148.title: The unbroken reading
148.hook: the whole Granth read aloud without a break, taking about forty-eight hours
148.howItsDone: For gurpurabs, family occasions and times of grief or thanks, Sikhs hold an akhand path: a team of readers takes turns to read the whole Guru Granth Sahib aloud without a break, over about forty-eight hours, ending with the bhog.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Nanak's gurpurab, lamps on the full moon of Katak. Your line was the light that came. Who did you think of when you switched on a light? Day one hundred forty-eight.

It's three in the morning in a gurdwara. The hall is almost empty. The lights are low. Outside, the city is asleep. But at the front, one person is sitting behind the Guru Granth Sahib, reading aloud, steadily, page after page. A few people sit wrapped in shawls, listening. In an hour or two, someone else will slide in beside the reader, pick up the line mid-sentence, and carry on, without a single second of silence in between. It started two days ago. It won't stop until the last page.
screen: `3 A.M., THE HALL NEARLY EMPTY.` → `ONE VOICE, READING ON.` → `NOT A SECOND OF SILENCE.`

segments.voice: It's an akhand path. Akhand means unbroken, undivided. Path means reading, recitation. So it's the unbroken reading: the whole Guru Granth Sahib, all 1,430 angs, read aloud from beginning to end without any break. It takes about forty-eight hours. No one person can do it alone, so a team of readers, called pathis, take turns in shifts. When one reader's time is up, the next sits beside them and takes over the words mid-flow, so the reading is never interrupted. Families and gurdwaras hold an akhand path for the big moments: gurpurabs, as you heard yesterday, and Vaisakhi, but also a wedding, a new baby, a new house, a death in the family, or simply to give thanks. It begins with Ardas and karah prashad. It ends with the bhog, the completion: the last pages are read, then Anand Sahib, Ardas, a hukamnama and prashad, often followed by langar. Nobody is expected to listen to all forty-eight hours. People drop in, sit for a while, leave, come back. Some stay up through the night to keep the readers company. What matters is that the word keeps sounding, through the day and the dark, unbroken. There's another way too: a sahaj path, a steady reading of the whole Granth at your own pace, over weeks or months. Families sometimes do this at home. Both come from the same wish: to hear the whole of the Guru's word, from Japji at the start to the last page, in order, all the way through.
screen: `AKHAND — UNBROKEN. PATH — READING.` · `1,430 ANGS, ABOUT 48 HOURS.` · `READERS TAKE TURNS MID-LINE.` · `THE BHOG, THE COMPLETION.` · then, large: `UNBROKEN.`

segments.voice: Today, find a recording of Gurbani being read, a path, and give it ten minutes at some point: on a walk, while cooking, before sleep. For now, begin with these two minutes. Play it if you can, or just sit. Imagine yourself at three in the morning in that nearly empty hall, wrapped in a shawl, listening to a voice that hasn't stopped for a day and a half. You don't need to understand. Just keep it company. The bell holds the time.
Akhand path. The unbroken reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib, about forty-eight hours, readers taking turns so the word never stops.
Your line: unbroken. Today, choose one small thing to keep going all day, a kindness, a patience, a word under the breath, and see if you can leave it unbroken until bed. Day one hundred forty-eight.

149.title: Guru Gobind Singh's gurpurab
149.hook: his birth is celebrated in winter with kirtan and processions
149.howItsDone: Sikhs celebrate Guru Gobind Singh's gurpurab in December or January with an akhand path, nagar kirtan, kirtan and langar; large gatherings are held at Takht Sri Patna Sahib, his birthplace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the akhand path, the unbroken reading. Your line was unbroken. What did you manage to keep going all day? Today, another gurpurab, in the middle of winter. Day one hundred forty-nine.

A nurse who's gentle with patients and fierce with bad doctors. A grandmother who writes poetry and once faced down a landlord. People get sorted into boxes all the time: the soft ones, the tough ones. The tenth Guru doesn't fit in either box. His poetry fills much of the Sikh morning prayers, and he led armies into battle. Sikhs celebrate his birthday in the heart of winter. Today, Guru Gobind Singh's gurpurab.
screen: `GENTLE AND FIERCE AT ONCE.` → `POET AND COMMANDER.` → `A BIRTHDAY IN WINTER.`

segments.voice: Guru Gobind Singh was born in 1666 in Patna, in eastern India, where a great gurdwara, one of the five Takhts, the seats of Sikh authority, now stands. His gurpurab falls in December or January, and it's kept the way you'd now expect: an akhand path, a nagar kirtan through the streets, kirtan and langar, and at Patna Sahib, pilgrims from far away. The exact date moves from year to year, and different Sikh calendars have calculated it differently; Sikhs have debated that, but not the celebration itself. Now the sword and the song. You've already met his words on this path: Jaap Sahib's galloping praise, the savaiyas that say without love, nothing, Chaupai asking to be kept under God's hand. He wrote in more than one language, and tradition says he kept poets at his court. And he was also a military leader who fought many battles to defend his people, created the Khalsa, and lost his father and all four of his sons in those years of persecution. How do the two fit? Sikhs call the ideal sant sipahi: saint-soldier. Devotion first, and courage in its service. In a Persian letter to the emperor Aurangzeb, the Zafarnama, Guru Gobind Singh says, in paraphrase, that when every other means has failed, it is right to take up the sword. Every other means first. And then there's a line from his Akal Ustat. In paraphrase: recognize the whole human race as one. That's the song the sword was meant to protect.
screen: `BORN IN PATNA, 1666.` · `A WINTER GURPURAB.` · `SANT SIPAHI — SAINT-SOLDIER.` · `THE WHOLE HUMAN RACE AS ONE.` · then, large: `SWORD AND SONG.`

segments.voice: Read one line of his. Here's the one to hold: recognize the whole human race as one. Say it silently, slowly, three times. Then think of one group of people you find hard to see as your own, whoever it is for you. Just hold them in the line for a few breaths. Not agreeing with everything. Just human, one kind with you. If you pray, you can hold them before God. The bell holds the time.
Guru Gobind Singh's gurpurab. The tenth Guru's birthday, kept in winter with kirtan and processions: the poet-commander, sword and song.
Your line: sword and song. Today, be gentle where you'd usually be hard, and brave where you'd usually go quiet, once each. Day one hundred forty-nine.

150.title: Guru Arjan's martyrdom day
150.hook: in the June heat Sikhs hand out cold sweetened water to passers-by
150.howItsDone: On and around the anniversary of Guru Arjan's martyrdom in June, Sikhs set up chhabeels, stalls handing out chilled sweetened drinks free to passers-by, alongside kirtan and prayers at the gurdwara.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Gobind Singh's gurpurab, the poet and commander. Your line was sword and song. Where were you gentle, and where were you brave? Today, a harder day in the Sikh year, and a surprising way to keep it. Day one hundred fifty.
screen: `GURU GOBIND SINGH'S GURPURAB — SWORD AND SONG.`

segments.voice: The night before, somebody's garage fills up with bags of ice. Big steel drums get rinsed out with a hose. There's a crate of milk, a sack of sugar, maybe a bottle of rose syrup, and a stack of paper cups as tall as a child. By mid-morning there's a table at a busy corner, it's well over a hundred degrees, and a line of teenagers is standing in the traffic with trays, waving cars down. On day sixty-four, you were the driver being handed a cup. Today, step around to the other side of the table.
screen: `ICE AND STEEL DRUMS, THE NIGHT BEFORE.` → `TRAYS HELD OUT INTO THE TRAFFIC.` → `THE OTHER SIDE OF THE TABLE.`

segments.voice: The stall is called a chhabeel. The word is usually traced to the Arabic sabil, a public water fountain given as charity, the kind built in Muslim cities from Cairo to Istanbul; a free drink of water is honored on more than one path. You already know whose day it is. On days sixty-three and sixty-four you met Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, held in Lahore in the summer of 1606, the first Sikh shaheed, and the line he held to: your will is sweet. Today isn't the story again. It's how the Sikh year keeps it. The anniversary falls in the hottest weeks, in May or June, depending on which calendar a gurdwara follows. Inside, there is kirtan of his hymns and an Ardas. Outside, the chhabeel. Here is how one actually runs. The drink is often kachi lassi: water with a little milk and sugar, sometimes rose syrup, poured over ice in those steel drums. It's handed out with both hands, to anyone, without asking a name or a faith. Truck drivers, police officers, schoolkids, strangers. A good chhabeel ends up with more helpers than it planned, because people walking past stop to pour. Some run for an afternoon, some for a week. Notice who holds the trays: very often the young. That's how a memory four hundred years old gets handed on. Not as a lecture about cruelty, but as a job: standing in the heat, cooling someone else.
screen: `CHHABEEL — FROM SABIL, A FREE FOUNTAIN.` · `GURU ARJAN'S DAY, IN THE HEAT.` · `KACHI LASSI, ICE AND BOTH HANDS.` · `A MEMORY HANDED ON AS A JOB.` · then, large: `COOL WATER FOR ANYONE.`

segments.voice: Give someone a cold drink, today if you can. For now, get yourself a glass of cool water, if one's near, and hold it. Feel the cold in your hands. Take one slow sip. Think of someone who's worn out, overheated, overworked today: a delivery driver, a coworker, someone at home. Picture handing them this glass, and their face as they take it. If you pray, you can remember Guru Arjan's calm. The bell holds the time.
Chhabeel. A stall of cold sweetened drinks given free to passers-by, remembering Guru Arjan, who was martyred in the heat.
Your line: cool water for anyone. Today, hand someone a cold drink, a delivery driver, a neighbor, a stranger, and ask nothing back. Day one hundred fifty.

151.title: Bandi Chhor Divas
151.hook: lamps are lit to remember Guru Hargobind's release from Gwalior, at Diwali time
151.howItsDone: On Bandi Chhor Divas, which falls at Diwali time, Sikhs light lamps and candles at home and in gurdwaras; the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar is illuminated and fireworks are set off over its pool.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Arjan's martyrdom day, and a cup of cold water on a hot road. Your line was cool water for anyone. Did someone get a drink from you, or did you at least notice who might need one? Day one hundred fifty-one.

Autumn, and across much of India the lamps come out. Diwali: rows of little clay lamps on windowsills, fireworks, boxes of sweets passed over walls to the neighbors. Hindus light them for Rama coming home, and for Lakshmi. Jains light them for Mahavira. On the same nights, Sikhs are lighting lamps too, for a story of their own, one you've already heard on this path. It's about a prison, a Guru who wouldn't leave alone, and a cloak. Today, what the Sikh year does with it.
screen: `LAMPS ON EVERY WINDOWSILL.` → `THE SAME NIGHTS, DIFFERENT STORIES.` → `A PRISON, AND A CLOAK.`

segments.voice: The day is called Bandi Chhor Divas. Bandi means a prisoner. Chhor means to set free. Divas is day. The day of the one who freed the prisoners. On day sixty-seven you heard the story. Tradition says Guru Hargobind, held by the emperor Jahangir in the fort at Gwalior, would not leave without the fifty-two rajas imprisoned with him, and walked out with every one of them holding a tassel of his cloak. Today isn't the story again. It's how the Sikh year keeps it. Sikhs remember that when he reached Amritsar, people lit lamps to welcome him, and it was Diwali time. So the day moves with Diwali, each autumn. At the Harmandir Sahib, that evening is the great one of the year. Ledges, railings and walkways are lined with lamps and strings of light, the whole building shimmers on the water, and fireworks open over the pool. A Punjabi saying puts it simply: dal and roti at home, but Diwali in Amritsar. At home, families set little lamps along walls and windowsills, share sweets, and go to the gurdwara. And inside the Gwalior fort itself there is now a gurdwara, called Data Bandi Chhor, where the Guru is remembered at the place he was held. Notice what all those lamps are for. Not an escape. A refusal to be free alone. The Guru's own release was a door, and he held it open until everyone behind him was through. And on those nights, Sikh and Hindu lamps burn on neighboring windowsills, each for its own story.
screen: `BANDI — PRISONER. CHHOR — SET FREE.` · `THE CLOAK, FROM DAY SIXTY-SEVEN.` · `DAL AND ROTI AT HOME, DIWALI IN AMRITSAR.` · `NOT FREE ALONE.` · then, large: `BANDI CHHOR.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is a lamp. If there's a candle or a tea light nearby, and it's safe, light it now. If not, picture one: small, steady, a little flicker at the top. Then think of someone who got free of something. Out of a hospital. Out of a bad job, a hard year, a debt, a cell. Hold them in that light for a while. If someone you know is still waiting to get free, hold them too, right beside the first. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them. The bell holds the time.
Bandi Chhor. The liberator of prisoners: a name for Guru Hargobind, who would not leave the fort at Gwalior without the fifty-two.
Your line: light for the freed. Sometime today, when you're let out of something, a meeting, a long line, a waiting room, hold the door for whoever is behind you. Day one hundred fifty-one.

152.title: Hola Mohalla
152.hook: at Anandpur, the day after Holi, mock battles, gatka and poetry fill the fields
152.howItsDone: At Hola Mohalla, held at Anandpur Sahib the day after Holi, Sikhs gather for several days of gatka, horsemanship, kirtan, poetry and langar, ending with a large procession; Nihang Singhs lead many of the martial displays.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bandi Chhor: a Guru who wouldn't leave the fort without the fifty-two. Your line was light for the freed. Did you hold a door for anyone? Day one hundred fifty-two.

A wide field in March. The day before, much of north India played Holi: colored powder everywhere, everyone pink and green and laughing. The next morning, at Anandpur Sahib in Punjab, something else begins. Horses thunder across the open ground. A rider in a tall blue turban stands up on two galloping horses at once. Pairs face off with sticks and small shields, spinning, blocking, grinning. Somewhere a poet is reciting to a crowd. Somewhere else a langar is feeding everyone who turns up. It's loud and dusty and joyful. It's Hola Mohalla.
screen: `HOLI, THE DAY BEFORE.` → `HORSES, STICKS AND SHIELDS.` → `A POET, A LANGAR, A CROWD.`

segments.voice: Hola Mohalla goes back to Guru Gobind Singh. Tradition says that around 1701, at Anandpur, he called the Sikhs together the day after Holi, not for colored powder but for drills and mock battles. People explain the name in more than one way. Hola is often linked to Holi, and also to halla, a charge. Mohalla is usually taken as an organized column, like a company on the march. Either way the picture is the same: a festival of movement. Why would a Guru do that? Remember the times. Guru Arjan and Guru Tegh Bahadur had both been executed. The Khalsa had been founded just a couple of years before. Sikhs remember that Sikhs remember that Guru Gobind Singh wanted a people who could defend themselves and others, and who weren't ruled by fear. So he took a season of play and pointed it at courage and skill. The play stayed. It's still a game and still a joy, but it trains the body. Today the festival runs over several days. There's gatka, the Sikh art of stick and sword. There's horsemanship, much of it from the Nihang Singhs, in deep blue, who keep the old martial ways alive. There's kirtan, and there are gatherings of poets, as there were, tradition says, at Guru Gobind Singh's court. And it closes with a great procession. Underneath is an idea you've met before: the saint-soldier. In Sikh teaching, devotion and strength aren't opposites, and a body that can run, stand and protect belongs to a life given to the Name. Hola Mohalla puts that on an open field and lets it be fun. Strength, in joy, not in anger.
screen: `THE DAY AFTER HOLI, AT ANANDPUR.` · `HOLA — A CHARGE. MOHALLA — A COLUMN.` · `PLAY, POINTED AT COURAGE.` · `GATKA, HORSES AND POETRY.` · then, large: `THE SAINT-SOLDIER.`

segments.voice: Today's practice moves. Stand up if you can. Roll your shoulders back. Shake out your hands. March gently in place, or step side to side. If you're sitting, lift your arms and sweep them slowly, like you're parting tall grass. Keep it light: this is a festival, not a workout. Let your breath keep time with your body. If you pray, let Waheguru ride on the breath. Notice the strength you have today, however much or little it is, and enjoy it. Then slow down, and let the body settle. The bell holds the time.
Hola Mohalla. The festival of mock battles, gatka and poetry at Anandpur, the day after Holi, begun by Guru Gobind Singh.

Your line: strength, in joy. Use your body for something today and let yourself enjoy it: the stairs, a fast walk, carrying the groceries in one trip. Strong and glad at the same time. Day one hundred fifty-two.

153.title: Maghi at Muktsar
153.hook: the fair at Muktsar in January remembers the Forty Liberated
153.howItsDone: On Maghi, in mid-January, Sikhs gather at Sri Muktsar Sahib for a large fair, bathe in the sacred pool, and remember the Chali Mukte, the Forty Liberated, with kirtan, prayers and langar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hola Mohalla: horses, gatka and poetry the day after Holi. Your line was strength, in joy. Did your body get to do something glad? Day one hundred fifty-three.

The night before Maghi, Punjab lights bonfires. It's Lohri: people circle the fire, toss in sesame and popcorn, and sing, and in some homes a pot of rice simmers slowly in sugarcane juice, to be eaten cold the next morning. That next morning is the first of the winter month of Magh. And in one town in Punjab, Sri Muktsar Sahib, it's the day of a huge fair, with crowds walking in from the cold toward a pool. You've already met the men that pool is named for.
screen: `LOHRI FIRES, THE NIGHT BEFORE.` → `THE FIRST MORNING OF MAGH.` → `CROWDS WALKING TOWARD A POOL.`

segments.voice: The fair is called Maghi, because it falls on the first day of Magh, a winter month in the Punjabi calendar, usually in mid-January. Across Punjab it's a winter feast day. At Muktsar it's more. On day ninety-one you heard why. Tradition says forty Sikhs left the besieged Guru and signed a paper saying they were no longer his Sikhs; Mai Bhago shamed them and rode back with them; at the pool of Khidrana all forty fell; and Mahan Singh, dying, asked for the paper to be torn, and the Guru tore it. Today isn't the story again. It's how a town keeps it. Khidrana became Muktsar, the pool of liberation, and on Maghi the crowds come to that pool. People bathe in it, in January water, early in the day. Then they go round the town's gurdwaras, each tied to a piece of the story. One is called Tuti Gandhi Sahib. Tuti means broken; gandhi, tied. The broken, tied again. Tradition places it where the paper was torn. Another, Shaheed Ganj, marks where the forty were cremated. There's kirtan, langar for whoever comes, and stalls and noise along the streets. It's a fair, after all. And the forty are not only remembered once a year. In the Ardas, the prayer that closes Sikh worship, they're named every day: the Chali Mukte, the forty liberated ones. Look at what a whole town has chosen to remember. Not people who never left. People who left, and came back anyway.
screen: `MAGHI — THE FIRST DAY OF MAGH.` · `THE FORTY, FROM DAY NINETY-ONE.` · `TUTI GANDHI — BROKEN, TIED AGAIN.` · `ONCE A YEAR, AND EVERY DAY.` · then, large: `CHALI MUKTE — THE FORTY LIBERATED.`

segments.voice: Settle, and think of a place you go back to. Not one you left in anger; just one you return to: a hometown street, a lake you swim in each summer, a grave you visit, a table where the same people gather every year. See yourself arriving. Notice what has stayed the same, and what has changed, including you. Stay a while with the coming back. If you pray, you can hold that place and its people in Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Maghi. The first day of the winter month of Magh, when the fair at Muktsar remembers the Forty Liberated.

Your line: come back, anyway. Today, go back to one small thing you dropped, a practice, a call, a page, and do it once. No speech needed. And if someone comes back to you, let them in without one. Day one hundred fifty-three.

154.title: Shaheedi Jor Mela
154.hook: in December Sikhs gather at Fatehgarh Sahib to remember the younger Sahibzade
154.howItsDone: In late December, Sikhs gather at Fatehgarh Sahib for the Shaheedi Jor Mela with kirtan, prayers, langar and a procession; some families observe the week in mourning, sleeping on the floor and keeping celebrations away.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maghi, and the Forty Liberated who came back. Your line was come back, anyway. Did you send that small message, or at least look at the door? Day one hundred fifty-four.

In the last week of December, while much of the world is between holidays, the roads around a town in Punjab called Fatehgarh Sahib fill with people. Huge crowds come, on foot, in buses, on tractor trolleys carrying half a village. But it isn't a celebration. Nobody is dressed for a party, there are no fireworks, and the mood is quiet, almost hushed. They've come to remember two little boys and their grandmother.
screen: `A TOWN FULL OF PEOPLE IN DECEMBER.` → `NOT A CELEBRATION.` → `TWO BOYS AND THEIR GRANDMOTHER.`

segments.voice: The gathering is the Shaheedi Jor Mela. Shaheedi means of the martyrs. Jor mela is a gathering, a coming together. On day ninety you heard what it remembers. Tradition says the Guru's mother, Mata Gujri, and his two youngest sons, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, were handed over to the governor of Sirhind and held in a cold tower; the boys refused to give up their faith and were bricked into a wall and put to death; and their grandmother died in the tower. Today isn't the story again. It's the place, and the days. The town is now called Fatehgarh Sahib, after the younger boy. Gurdwara Fatehgarh Sahib stands where tradition places the wall. Close by, Gurdwara Thanda Burj keeps the memory of the cold tower. A little way off is Gurdwara Jyoti Sarup, on the ground that a merchant named Todar Mal, tradition says, bought for their cremation by covering it with gold coins. The mela moves between these places over several days at the end of December: unbroken readings, kirtan in tents, langar along the roads, and a long procession. Far from Fatehgarh, some families keep the whole week in mourning at home: no parties, no sweets, a mattress on the floor instead of a bed. One more name is honored in these days: Malerkotla, whose Nawab, Sher Muhammad Khan, protested in open court that children must not be punished. People sometimes say the boys were too young to understand what they were choosing. Sikhs remember it the other way: small, and yet they would not bend.
screen: `SHAHEEDI — OF THE MARTYRS.` · `THE STORY, FROM DAY NINETY.` · `THE WALL, THE TOWER, THE GOLD.` · `A WEEK ON THE FLOOR.` · then, large: `THE YOUNGER SAHIBZADE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is quiet. No doing. Sit still, and think of the two boys and their grandmother. You don't need to picture the wall. Picture them together, her hand resting on each small head. Then let the circle widen to children anywhere who are carrying things too heavy for them. If you pray, you can hold them all in Waheguru. If you don't, simply keep them company in the silence, the way you'd sit beside someone who is grieving. The bell holds the time.
Shaheedi Jor Mela. The gathering at Fatehgarh Sahib each December to remember the younger Sahibzade and Mata Gujri.

Your line: small, and unbending. Today, notice a child's courage: saying sorry first, trying again, telling the truth when it costs. And look back at this week: an unbroken reading, a Guru's birthday, cool water, lamps for the freed, strength in joy, and coming back. Day one hundred fifty-four.

screen: `DAY 154 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: GURU TEGH BAHADUR'S MARTYRDOM DAY.`
